note: The counted exception to fill-empty-only: every theme here exists in the source with a band-suffixed description (the documented content debt); this promotion replaces exactly those rows with five authored sentences per theme. The normaliser refuses any other target. Track names, prefixes, codes, credentials and transfer checks are untouched.

themes.description: Counting degrees of freedom on a real mechanism and predicting what it cannot reach.

bands.K–2: Move a toy arm or a door and count the ways it can move, then find one place it cannot reach.
bands.3–5: Count the ways a real mechanism can move and show a classmate a position it cannot get to.
bands.6–8: Count the degrees of freedom on a real rig or kit and demonstrate an unreachable pose to a checker.
bands.9–10: Count them on a physical rig and demonstrate an unreachable pose.
bands.11–12: Count the degrees of freedom on a real machine for its operators, document the unreachable poses, and put them in its operating notes.

themes.description: Forward and inverse kinematics understood by moving something with your hands first.

bands.K–2: Move your own arm to touch a spot, then say what each joint did to get there.
bands.3–5: Predict where a toy arm's hand will end up when you set its joints, then check by measuring.
bands.6–8: Predict an end-effector position on a real kit arm from its joint angles, then measure it and explain the difference.
bands.9–10: Predict an end-effector position, then measure it.
bands.11–12: Predict end-effector positions for a real machine, measure them, and quantify the error for the people who program it.

themes.theme: Sensors and what each actually senses
themes.description: What each sensor physically responds to, and the thing it is routinely assumed to sense instead.

bands.K–2: Say what a light sensor, a button and a distance sensor each really notice.
bands.3–5: For two sensors on a kit robot, say what each physically measures and one thing people wrongly think it measures.
bands.6–8: For three real sensors, state the physical quantity each responds to and one common misreading, checked by a teacher.
bands.9–10: For three sensors, state the physical quantity and one common misreading.
bands.11–12: For every sensor on a real machine, state the physical quantity and the misreading it invites, in the machine's documentation.

themes.description: Actuators, the force available, and the limits that are structural rather than software.

bands.K–2: Find what stops a toy motor lifting something heavy, and say whether it is the motor or the arm.
bands.3–5: On a kit robot, find which part gives out first when it lifts too much, and say why.
bands.6–8: Identify the limiting component in a real actuator chain on a kit or rig, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify the limiting component in a real actuator chain.
bands.11–12: Identify the limiting component in a real machine's actuator chain and document the structural limit for its operators.

themes.theme: Power, batteries and the hour they last
themes.description: Power budgets, and why the stated runtime and the observed runtime differ.

bands.K–2: Time how long a toy runs on one charge and compare it with what the box says.
bands.3–5: Measure how long a kit robot really runs under load and compare it with the stated time.
bands.6–8: Measure actual runtime of a real kit or rig under load and reconcile it with the specification, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Measure actual runtime under load and reconcile it with the specification.
bands.11–12: Measure a real machine's runtime under real load, reconcile it with the specification, and publish the honest figure for its users.

themes.description: Calibrating a real machine, and the error that calibration cannot remove.

bands.K–2: Set a toy scale or sensor to zero before using it and check it reads right on something known.
bands.3–5: Calibrate a kit sensor against something known and say how far off it still is.
bands.6–8: Calibrate a real rig and quantify the residual error, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Calibrate a rig and quantify the residual error.
bands.11–12: Calibrate a real machine, quantify the residual error, and write the error into its operating tolerance.

themes.theme: The mechanical failure you can hear
themes.description: Mechanical failure has an acoustic signature before it has a functional one.

bands.K–2: Listen to a machine that is working well and one that is not, and say what is different.
bands.3–5: Find a fault in a kit mechanism by its sound before you look at it.
bands.6–8: Identify a fault on a real rig by sound and confirm it by inspection, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify a fault by sound and confirm it by inspection.
bands.11–12: Identify faults by sound on real machines over a month and record which ones inspection confirmed.

themes.description: Maintenance as a scheduled discipline that prevents the failure rather than diagnosing it.

bands.K–2: Make a checklist to look after a class machine or bike, and follow it for a week.
bands.3–5: Write a maintenance list for a kit robot and follow it for a term.
bands.6–8: Produce and follow a maintenance schedule for one real machine, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Produce and follow a maintenance schedule for one machine.
bands.11–12: Produce and run a maintenance schedule for a real machine for a term, and show the failure it prevented.

themes.description: Reading a schematic well enough to find a component you have never seen.

bands.K–2: Use a simple drawing of a toy to find a part you have never seen.
bands.3–5: Find two parts on a kit robot using only its diagram.
bands.6–8: Locate three components on real hardware using only the schematic, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Locate three components on hardware using only the schematic.
bands.11–12: Locate components on an unfamiliar real machine using only its schematic, and correct the schematic where it was wrong.

themes.description: Building something that moves, which is where every abstraction gets tested.

bands.K–2: Build something that moves the same way every time, and show what it cannot do.
bands.3–5: Build a kit mechanism that repeats one motion and write down its limits.
bands.6–8: Build a mechanism that performs one repeatable motion and document its limits, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Build a mechanism that performs one repeatable motion, and document its limits.
bands.11–12: Build a mechanism for a real use, document its repeatability and limits, and have somebody else operate it from the documentation.

themes.description: Guarding, interlocks and emergency stops: what each protects and the order they act in.

bands.K–2: Find the stop button on a class machine and say what it does.
bands.3–5: On a kit robot or class machine, find each guard and stop and say what it protects.
bands.6–8: Trace the stop circuit on a real cell or rig and identify every trigger, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Trace the stop circuit on a real cell and identify every trigger.
bands.11–12: Trace the stop circuit on a real cell, identify every trigger, and verify each one actually stops the machine.

themes.theme: The envelope and staying out of it
themes.description: The working envelope, how it is defined, and why standing in it is the recurring incident.

bands.K–2: Mark on the floor where a moving toy could reach and stay outside the line.
bands.3–5: Mark the space a kit robot can reach and show the safe way to approach it.
bands.6–8: Mark the working envelope of a real machine physically and demonstrate the safe approach, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Mark the envelope physically and demonstrate the safe approach.
bands.11–12: Mark the envelope of a real cell, demonstrate the safe approach to its operators, and record it in the cell's procedure.

themes.description: Speed and separation monitoring, and the assumptions underneath the safe distance.

bands.K–2: Say why a fast-moving thing needs more space around it than a slow one.
bands.3–5: Work out how far away you need to stand from a moving kit robot and why.
bands.6–8: State the assumptions behind one published separation distance, with a checker.
bands.9–10: State the assumptions behind one published separation distance.
bands.11–12: State the assumptions behind a real cell's separation distance and check each one on the floor.

themes.theme: A collaborative robot is still a machine
themes.description: A collaborative robot has reduced force, not zero force, and the distinction gets people hurt.

bands.K–2: Say why a robot that is made to work near people can still hurt someone.
bands.3–5: Explain why a robot with a force limit still needs care, using a kit example.
bands.6–8: Demonstrate the force limit on a real collaborative machine or kit and state what it does not protect against, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Demonstrate the force limit and state what it does not protect against.
bands.11–12: Demonstrate the force limit on a real collaborative robot to its operators and document what it does not protect against.

themes.description: Isolating energy before work, including the stored energy people forget.

bands.K–2: Before fixing a toy, take the batteries out and tell an adult it is safe.
bands.3–5: Switch off and unplug a kit robot before working on it, and find any energy still stored.
bands.6–8: Perform a full isolation on a real machine and identify every stored energy source, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Perform a full isolation and identify every stored energy source.
bands.11–12: Perform and verify a full isolation on a real machine under a written lockout procedure, and train somebody else in it.

themes.theme: Risk assessment before the first run
themes.description: Risk assessment before the first run, written by the people who will operate it.

bands.K–2: Before running a machine you built, list what could go wrong and how you will stop it.
bands.3–5: Write a risk assessment for a kit robot before its first run.
bands.6–8: Produce a risk assessment for a real cell or rig and have an operator challenge it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Produce a risk assessment for a real cell and have an operator challenge it.
bands.11–12: Produce the risk assessment for a real cell with its operators and have it signed before the first run.

themes.description: A documented case where the safety system did its job, read for what made it work.

bands.K–2: Find one story where a safety feature stopped an accident, and say what worked.
bands.3–5: Present one case where a machine's safety system worked, and say which part did it.
bands.6–8: Present one documented case and identify the specific control that held, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Present one case and identify the specific control that held.
bands.11–12: Present a documented case to a real team and identify the control that held and whether their cell has it.

themes.description: A documented case where it did not, read without hindsight bias.

bands.K–2: Find one story where a machine hurt someone, and say what could have stopped it.
bands.3–5: Present one case where a safety system failed, and say what people could have known before.
bands.6–8: Present one documented case and identify what was knowable at the time, without hindsight, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Present one case and identify what was knowable at the time.
bands.11–12: Present a documented failure to a real team, identify what was knowable, and check their cell for the same gap.

themes.theme: Training somebody else on the cell
themes.description: Training somebody else on a cell, which is where your own gaps surface.

bands.K–2: Teach a classmate how to use a class machine safely, and watch them do it.
bands.3–5: Train a classmate on a kit robot and be judged on how well they use it.
bands.6–8: Train one person on a real rig and be assessed on their competence, not yours, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Train one person and be assessed on their competence, not yours.
bands.11–12: Train a real operator on a real cell against a written competence standard, and be assessed on their performance.

themes.theme: The stop you should have hit
themes.description: The stop you hesitated on, and building the reflex before you need it.

bands.K–2: Practise pressing the stop button on a class machine until you do it without thinking.
bands.3–5: Practise stopping a kit robot until it is automatic, and time yourself.
bands.6–8: Rehearse the stop on a real rig until it is automatic and log the response time, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Rehearse the stop until it is automatic, and log the response time.
bands.11–12: Rehearse the stop on a real cell with its operators, log response times, and repeat until every operator meets the standard.

themes.description: Open loop and closed loop, felt on a real system rather than derived on a board.

bands.K–2: Try steering a toy with your eyes closed and then open, and say which is which.
bands.3–5: Run a kit robot task with and without its sensor feedback and say what changed.
bands.6–8: Run the same task on a real rig both ways — open loop and closed loop — and measure the difference, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Run the same task both ways and measure the difference.
bands.11–12: Run a real machine task both ways, measure the difference, and write the case for the control the task needs.

themes.description: Tuning a system that oscillates, and why the fast solution is usually the wrong one.

bands.K–2: Make a wobbling toy settle by changing one thing at a time, and say what helped.
bands.3–5: Adjust a kit robot that overshoots until it settles, changing one setting at a time.
bands.6–8: Tune a real loop on a rig and document each change and its effect, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Tune a real loop and document each change and its effect.
bands.11–12: Tune a real machine's loop, document each change and effect, and hand the record to the next person who tunes it.

themes.description: The sense-plan-act cycle, its timing, and what happens when one stage is late.

bands.K–2: Act out sense, plan, act as a game: look, decide, move — and say what happens if you decide too late.
bands.3–5: Time the sense, plan and act steps of a kit robot and find the slowest.
bands.6–8: Instrument the sense-plan-act cycle on a real rig and find the stage that limits it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Instrument the cycle and find the stage that limits it.
bands.11–12: Instrument the cycle on a real machine, find the limiting stage, and propose the change with its measured effect.

themes.theme: When the plan meets the world
themes.description: The gap between a plan made in a model and a world that was not in the model.

bands.K–2: Plan a route for a toy across the floor, then put a book in the way and see what happens.
bands.3–5: Run a planned kit-robot move with an obstacle added and write what went wrong.
bands.6–8: Run a planned motion on a real rig in a disturbed environment and record the divergence, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Run a planned motion in a disturbed environment and record the divergence.
bands.11–12: Run a real planned motion under real disturbance, record the divergence, and change the plan or the model on the evidence.

themes.description: Teleoperation, latency, and the operator behaviours that latency produces.

bands.K–2: Steer a toy while a friend delays passing on your instructions, and say what you did differently.
bands.3–5: Drive a kit robot with a built-in delay and describe how you changed the way you drove.
bands.6–8: Operate a real rig under induced delay and describe how your own behaviour changed, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Operate under induced delay and describe how your own behaviour changed.
bands.11–12: Operate a real machine under measured delay, document the behaviours it produced, and write the operator guidance.

themes.description: Autonomy levels described by what the human must still do, not by marketing.

bands.K–2: For three machines you know, say what a person still has to do.
bands.3–5: Sort three real machines by how much a person still has to do, not by what the advert says.
bands.6–8: Classify three real systems by what the human is required to do, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Classify three real systems by what the human is required to do.
bands.11–12: Classify real systems for a real buyer or team by what the human must still do, against the marketing claim for each.

themes.description: Handover between human and machine, which is where most autonomy incidents occur.

bands.K–2: Practise handing a task to a friend with a clear 'you have it' and 'I have it'.
bands.3–5: Design a hand-over rule for a kit robot where the person must say they have taken over.
bands.6–8: Design and test a handover protocol with an explicit acknowledgement step on a real rig, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Design and test a handover protocol with an explicit acknowledgement step.
bands.11–12: Design, test and document a handover protocol for a real machine and its operators, including the acknowledgement step.

themes.theme: The failure mode you designed for
themes.description: The failure mode you designed for, and proving the design actually handles it.

bands.K–2: Make a toy do the safe thing when its sensor is covered, and show it working.
bands.3–5: Make a kit robot stop safely when a sensor fails, and prove it by making the sensor fail.
bands.6–8: Induce the anticipated failure on a real rig and verify the response, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Induce the anticipated failure and verify the response.
bands.11–12: Induce every anticipated failure on a real machine and verify each response on the record.

themes.theme: The failure mode you did not
themes.description: The failure mode you did not, and building the system so it is at least visible.

bands.K–2: Find one way your toy could go wrong that you had not thought of, and make it show a warning.
bands.3–5: Find one unhandled failure on a kit robot and add a way to see that it happened.
bands.6–8: Identify one unhandled failure on a real rig and add detection for it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify one unhandled failure and add detection for it.
bands.11–12: Identify unhandled failures on a real machine, add detection, and show the detection working in service.

themes.theme: Logging enough to explain a failure
themes.description: Logging enough to reconstruct a failure without logging so much that nobody reads it.

bands.K–2: Keep a simple log of what a toy did so you can explain why it stopped.
bands.3–5: Design what a kit robot should record so you can explain one failure afterwards.
bands.6–8: Define a logging policy for a real rig and reconstruct one incident from it alone, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Define a logging policy and reconstruct one incident from it alone.
bands.11–12: Define the logging policy for a real machine, reconstruct a real incident from the logs alone, and revise the policy from what was missing.

themes.theme: What an episode of robot data is
themes.description: What an episode of robot data actually contains, including what was captured incidentally.

bands.K–2: List everything a camera on a toy would see in one minute, including things you did not mean it to.
bands.3–5: List every stream a kit robot records in one run, including the ones nobody meant.
bands.6–8: Inventory every stream in one real episode of robot data, including the unintended ones, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Inventory every stream in one episode, including the unintended ones.
bands.11–12: Inventory every stream in a real dataset's episodes for the people who will use it, including what was captured incidentally.

themes.description: Consent before recording, from everybody in the space and not only the operator.

bands.K–2: Ask everyone in the room before recording, and say what the recording is for.
bands.3–5: Write a consent note for a class recording that says what is recorded and why.
bands.6–8: Produce the consent process for a real workspace recording, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Produce the consent process for a real workspace recording.
bands.11–12: Produce and run the consent process for a real workspace recording, with everybody in the space, before recording starts.

themes.description: A workspace is somebody’s workplace, and recording it is recording their working day.

bands.K–2: Say how you would feel if someone recorded your whole day, and what they should tell you.
bands.3–5: Write the notice you would want if your classroom were being recorded.
bands.6–8: Write the notice a worker in a real recorded space is owed and have one review it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write the notice a worker in that space is owed, and have one review it.
bands.11–12: Write the notice for a real workplace recording, have the workers review it, and change the recording to what they accept.

themes.description: Designing capture so faces are never recorded, rather than recorded and then removed.

bands.K–2: Set up a toy camera so it points where faces are not, and show it.
bands.3–5: Position a kit camera so it cannot see faces at all, rather than blurring them later.
bands.6–8: Demonstrate a capture configuration on a real rig where faces are not acquired at all, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Demonstrate a capture configuration where faces are not acquired at all.
bands.11–12: Design and verify a real capture configuration where faces are never acquired, and document it for the dataset's users.

themes.description: Constraint integrity: a dataset that preserves what was physically impossible in the scene.

bands.K–2: Say what a toy could not have done in a recording, and check the recording agrees.
bands.3–5: Check that a kit robot's recorded data never shows something physically impossible.
bands.6–8: Verify that one real dataset's physical constraints survived its processing pipeline, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Verify that one dataset's constraints survived its processing pipeline.
bands.11–12: Verify constraint integrity across a real dataset's pipeline and report every place it was lost.

themes.description: Labelling that survives independent review, with the ambiguous cases marked rather than guessed.

bands.K–2: Label pictures with a friend separately, then compare and mark the ones you disagree on.
bands.3–5: Label a small set of kit-robot data, swap with a classmate, and reconcile the differences.
bands.6–8: Label a sample, have it independently relabelled, and reconcile the disagreement, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Label a sample, have it independently relabelled, and reconcile the disagreement.
bands.11–12: Run a real labelling round with independent relabelling, reconcile the disagreements, and publish the ambiguity rate.

themes.theme: Who owns an episode you contributed
themes.description: Who owns an episode you contributed, and what the licence actually permits.

bands.K–2: Say who owns a drawing you made for a class display, and what they may do with it.
bands.3–5: Read the rules for a class data project and say what others may do with what you contributed.
bands.6–8: Read one dataset licence and state what a downstream user may do, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Read one dataset licence and state what a downstream user may do.
bands.11–12: Read a real dataset licence for real contributors, state what users may do, and correct the contributor notice where it was wrong.

themes.theme: Export, and where the data lands
themes.description: Export, jurisdiction, and where the data physically comes to rest.

bands.K–2: Say where a photo goes after you take it on a shared device.
bands.3–5: Trace where a class recording is stored, and who can reach it.
bands.6–8: Trace one dataset's path from capture to storage, naming each jurisdiction, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Trace one dataset's path from capture to storage, naming each jurisdiction.
bands.11–12: Trace a real dataset's path and jurisdictions for its owners, and document where it comes to rest.

themes.description: Withdrawal after the fact, and whether the architecture makes it possible at all.

bands.K–2: Ask for a recording of you to be deleted, and check that it was.
bands.3–5: Test whether a class data project can really remove one person's data when asked.
bands.6–8: Test a withdrawal request against a real pipeline and report where it fails, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Test a withdrawal request against a real pipeline and report where it fails.
bands.11–12: Test withdrawal against a real pipeline, report the failures to its owners, and verify the fix.

themes.theme: A dataset you would be happy to be in
themes.description: The standard: a dataset you would be content to appear in yourself.

bands.K–2: Say whether you would be happy to be in a class recording, and what would make it fair.
bands.3–5: Apply the test — would you be happy to be in it — to a class dataset and say what would change.
bands.6–8: Apply the test to a real dataset and state what would have to change, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Apply the test to a real dataset and state what would have to change.
bands.11–12: Apply the test to a real dataset with its owners, state what must change, and change it.

themes.theme: The job before the robot and after
themes.description: The job before automation and after, described by the person doing it rather than the vendor.

bands.K–2: Ask someone whose job changed because of a machine what it was like before and after.
bands.3–5: Interview an adult whose work a machine changed and write their account in their words.
bands.6–8: Interview somebody whose work was automated and write their account, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Interview somebody whose work was automated and write their account.
bands.11–12: Interview several people whose work was automated, write their accounts, and present them alongside the vendor's version.

themes.theme: Tasks that should not be automated
themes.description: Tasks that should not be automated, and the reasons that are not efficiency reasons.

bands.K–2: Say one job at school that a machine should not do, and why it is not about speed.
bands.3–5: Argue for one task at school that should stay with a person, for reasons that are not efficiency.
bands.6–8: Argue one such case for a real workplace you know, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Argue one such case in your own workplace.
bands.11–12: Argue the case for a real task in a real workplace to the people deciding, with reasons that are not efficiency.

themes.description: Retraining that starts before the equipment arrives, which is the only time it works.

bands.K–2: Say what a person should learn before a new machine arrives at their work.
bands.3–5: Draft a timeline of what people should learn before a machine is installed at a workplace you know.
bands.6–8: Draft a retraining timeline anchored to a real installation date, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Draft a retraining timeline anchored to an installation date.
bands.11–12: Draft and agree a retraining timeline with a real workplace before its installation date, and track it.

themes.theme: Being the person who maintains it
themes.description: Maintenance as a career rather than a consolation, and what it actually requires.

bands.K–2: Say what a person who looks after machines needs to know and be good at.
bands.3–5: List the skills a maintenance technician needs and mark the ones you have.
bands.6–8: Map the competencies of a real maintenance role and assess yourself against them, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Map the competencies of a maintenance role and assess yourself against them.
bands.11–12: Map the competencies of a real maintenance role with somebody who holds it, assess yourself, and plan the gap.

themes.description: Negotiating automation collectively, and what has historically been won.

bands.K–2: Say what workers might ask for when a machine comes to their workplace.
bands.3–5: Find one real agreement between workers and an employer about a machine, and say what workers got.
bands.6–8: Find one real agreement on automation and identify what was secured, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Find one real agreement and identify what was secured.
bands.11–12: Find real agreements on automation in a real sector and present what was secured to the people who might negotiate next.

themes.description: Measuring what changed, including the effects that were not in the business case.

bands.K–2: Say three things that change when a machine arrives, including one nobody planned.
bands.3–5: Design a way to measure what a machine changed at a workplace, including one effect the plan missed.
bands.6–8: Design the measurement for a real automation, including one effect the business case omitted, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Design the measurement, including one effect the business case omitted.
bands.11–12: Design and run the measurement for a real automation, including the omitted effects, and report the results honestly.

themes.theme: The skill that became more valuable
themes.description: The skill that became more valuable, and noticing it early enough to invest.

bands.K–2: Say one thing people are better at than machines, that matters more now.
bands.3–5: Name one skill in a trade that a machine made more valuable, and give evidence.
bands.6–8: Identify one such skill in a real trade and evidence the claim, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify one such skill in your trade and evidence the claim.
bands.11–12: Identify the skills a real automation made more valuable, evidence each, and advise the people who should invest in them.

themes.description: The skill that became less valuable, and saying so without pretending otherwise.

bands.K–2: Say one job a machine now does better, and what the person can do instead.
bands.3–5: Name one skill a machine made less valuable and describe an honest way to move on from it.
bands.6–8: Identify one such skill in a real trade and describe the honest transition from it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify one and describe the honest transition from it.
bands.11–12: Identify the skills a real automation made less valuable and write the honest transition for the people who hold them.

themes.description: Teaching a machine your trade, and what is lost in the demonstrations.

bands.K–2: Show a machine or a friend how to do a task by doing it, and say what they still would not know.
bands.3–5: Record yourself doing a task for a kit robot to copy, and list what it cannot learn from watching.
bands.6–8: Record a demonstration set on a real rig and state what the machine cannot learn from it, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Record a demonstration set and state what the machine cannot learn from it.
bands.11–12: Record demonstrations of a real trade skill for a real system and document, for its designers, what the demonstrations do not carry.

themes.theme: A workshop that keeps its people
themes.description: A workshop that adopted machines and kept its people, and the decisions that made that possible.

bands.K–2: Find a story of a workplace that got machines and kept its workers, and say how.
bands.3–5: Present one case of a workshop that automated and kept its people, and the choices that made it possible.
bands.6–8: Present one real case and identify the decisions that were not automatic, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Present one case and identify the decisions that were not automatic.
bands.11–12: Present a real case to a real workshop facing automation and identify the decisions open to them.

themes.theme: Voltage, current and what will hurt you
themes.description: The electrical quantities that matter on a real rig, and the ones that are dangerous.

bands.K–2: Say which things in the classroom are safe to touch and which have dangerous electricity.
bands.3–5: On a kit robot, point to the parts that could hurt you and say why.
bands.6–8: Identify the hazardous points on a real system, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify the hazardous points on a real system.
bands.11–12: Identify and label the hazardous points on a real machine for the people who work on it.
